in this session, you will explore the organization of the standards for mathematical content and how envisionmath common core © 2012 reflects the organization in its program design. you will connect depth of knowledge (dok) levels with the level of understanding that the standards for mathematical content require, and you will better understand how these standards reflect what is known about students’ mathematical learning progressions. click here to access the participant workbook. click here to access the common core state standards for mathematics (ccssm) document. (national governors association center for best practices, council of chief state school officers 2010)

college- and career-ready students • demonstrate independence • build strong content knowledge • respond to the various demands of audience, task, purpose, and discipline • comprehend as well as critique • value evidence • use technology and digital media strategically and capably • come to understand other perspectives and cultures (common core state standards initiative 2012b)

content organization envisionmath common core content is organized by domain. each topic teacher’s edition is color-coded to reflect this organization. on page 14 of your teacher’s program overview, you can see the organization at your own grade level. (pearson education, inc. 2012j, 14)

to teach the rigorous skills and knowledge called for in the standards for mathematical content, it is helpful to look at two frameworks or models that have been used to define rigor. bloom’s revised taxonomy depth of knowledge (dok)

bloom’s revised taxonomy bloom's revised taxonomy categorizes the thinking processes required by a learner when answering a question or approaching a task. (hess et al. 2009, 4) # 16 (overbaugh and schultz 2010)

create combining elements or ideas to engage in creative thinking or develop an original idea actions: put together elements to form a coherent whole, reorganize elements into new patterns/structures, generate, hypothesize, design, plan, construct, produce for a specific purpose (hess et al. 2009, 3)

evaluate judging the value of ideas, methods, and materials by developing and applying standards and criteria actions: judge based on criteria, check, detect inconsistencies or fallacies, judge, critique (hess et al. 2009, 3)

analyze breaking information down into its component elements actions: determine how parts relate, differentiate between, distinguish, focus, select, organize, outline, find coherence, deconstruct (for example: for bias or point of view) (hess et al. 2009, 3)
remember retrieving specific information from long-term memory actions: recognize, recall, locate, identify (hess et al. 2009, 3)
apply carrying out or using a procedure in a given situation actions: use, implement, carry out (hess et al. 2009, 3)

understand constructing meaning based on provided information actions: clarify, paraphrase, represent, translate, illustrate, provide examples, classify, categorize, summarize, generalize, infer a logical conclusion (such as from examples given), predict, match similar ideas, explain, compare/contrast, construct models (hess et al. 2009, 3)

depth of knowledge (dok) is a scale of cognitive demand measuring the knowledge level and complexity required by standards and assessments. it relates more closely to the depth of content understanding and the skills required to complete a task from beginning to end (such as planning, researching, or drawing conclusions). (hess 2006; webb et al. 2005; webb 2006) # 16

basic application of skill/concept: activities require that students use information or conceptual knowledge. they select appropriate procedures, follow two or more steps with decision points along the way, engage in routine problems, and organize or display data.

strategic thinking: activities require that students use reasoning and develop a plan or sequence of steps to approach the problem. they use decision making and provide justification, think abstractly and complexly, and understand that often more than one answer is possible.

extended thinking: activities require that students investigate or apply skills or concepts to real-world situations. they have time to research, think, process multiple conditions of the problem or task, and engage in non-routine manipulations that extend across disciplines or content areas and multiple sources.

cognitive rigor can be defined as the intersection of the complexity of the content, the cognitive engagement of students with that content, and the scope of the planned learning activities. to more accurately capture cognitive rigor, bloom’s revised taxonomy and dok have been combined in the cognitive rigor matrix. please review the matrix found in the participant workbook. (hess et al. 2009, 6) # 17
recall: activities require that students recall or recognize facts, information, concepts or procedures. problems are one-step, well-defined, and require straight algorithmic procedures.

Hello, and welcome to Get Ready to Read, the second session of the Reading Street 2011 Product Implementation Essentials Virtual Course.
In Session two we’ ll discuss the features of instruction that prepare students for reading during Get Ready to Read.
In this session, you’ ll also answer questions and complete activities that’ ll deepen your understanding of the Get Ready to Read instruction. These questions and activities are included in a Participant Workbook. Download the Participant Workbook by clicking Attachments in the upper corner of your screen.
